reader.title: Alleged lynching of Press Sams
bases: The only violence in the coverage is a reported or threatened lynching of Sams in Kentucky after his marriage to a white woman: McCoy hinted he was lynched (A4) and other dispatches said he fled to escape lynching (A5, A14).

No paper reports a killing as fact: the lynching rests on Deputy McCoy's intimation (A4) and 'probably' briefs (A12), while the Clinton report and other dispatches say Sams fled or left (A4, A5, A3, A13); no group, place or method of a lynching is described.

The marriage and McCoy's return of Flack are corroborated (A1, A4, A5, A13), but the lynching is contradicted by reports that Sams fled or was a fugitive (A3, A5, A13) and even within A4 by the Clinton report.

summary.text: The alleged lynching of Press Sams was an unconfirmed report, printed in white newspapers in October 1888, that Sams, a Black man who had married a white woman near Jacksonville, Illinois, had been lynched in Kentucky.

The claim rested on hints from the deputy, D. C. McCoy, as relayed by a Philadelphia Press special, while other reports of the same days said Sams had fled to escape lynching or had left for parts unknown.
The coverage dwelt mainly on the marriage across the color line.
On September 18, 1888, a Jacksonville dispatch reported that Hattie B. Flack, daughter of C. E. Flack of a St. Louis commission firm, had eloped with "Preston Sands, a colored man," and married him.
Sands had worked for the family for years until he was discharged for stealing, the dispatch said, and the couple took out a license in Springfield.
The Cleveland Gazette, which called the match a "social sensation" in Jacksonville society, named the groom "John Sams," her father's hired man, and said the couple were thought to be in Springfield.
Later reports called him Press or Pres Sams, the family's coachman or farm hand, and a "negro" or "mulatto."
Late in September, Deputy Sheriff D. C. McCoy of Jacksonville, described as an old friend of the family, set out on Sams's trail.
According to the Philadelphia Press special, he found the couple at a log cabin in the mountains near Clinton, Kentucky, living with the family of Sams's brother-in-law.
Other reports placed her arrest at Moscow, Kentucky, at the house of Jim Gahlson, described as Sams's brother-in-law.
The Press special said she gave way only when McCoy convinced her that Sams had another wife from whom he had never been divorced, and the Superior Times placed that wife at Union City, Tennessee.
McCoy brought her to St. Louis and turned her over to her father on or about October 1.
Sams was not brought back with her, and the papers disagreed about what had become of him.
No report of Sams's arrest, a bigamy prosecution, a body or an inquest was found in the coverage.
The latest item found, a Kansas brief of October 13, said only that he had fled "to escape lynchers."
The story ran in white papers from Illinois to California between September 18 and October 13, 1888.
The Philadelphia Press special, reprinted by the Washington Evening Star and the Wheeling Intelligencer, ran under the headline "She Married the Negro Coachman, and He Has Probably Been Lynched."
A California Associated Press version, headed "The Color Line," announced an "Alleged Lynching of a Negro Who Eloped with a White Girl."

The other dispatch, carried by the Memphis Appeal, the Indianapolis Journal and the Omaha Bee under headings such as "She Repents Her Folly" and "Tired of Her Negro Husband," said Sams fled and closed by saying the girl "now bitterly repents her folly."

Weekly news summaries then cut the story to a single line stating that "the bigamist has probably been lynched," a form that ran in the Maryland Evening Capital, the Martinsburg Herald and the Carbon Advocate.

Headlines treated the interracial marriage itself as the sensation, from the Rock Island Argus's "A Highly Colored Elopement" to its "Wasn't Even an Honest Negro," and a Kansas brief called Flack his "victim."
The Cleveland Gazette, a Black weekly, printed the marriage item in a column of race news without comment, and no item from it on the lynching report was found.

The only source for a lynching was McCoy, who, in the Press special's words, "refuses to say what became of Sams, but intimates that he was lynched to save the state the expense of his trial for bigamy."
The same special reported that the word at Clinton was that Sams "has left the country."

The St. Louis dispatch said he "fled to escape lynching," the Rock Island Argus called him a horse thief "now a fugitive in Kentucky," and the Superior Times said he had left her a week earlier "for parts unknown," after pawning her clothing.
The lynching version came from one officer's hint, never stated as fact, while the report from Clinton and several separate dispatches agreed that Sams had fled.

framing.detail: 'She Married the Negro Coachman, and He Has Probably Been Lynched' passed on McCoy's hint without question.
Headed 'The Color Line' and 'Alleged Lynching of a Negro Who Eloped with a White Girl'.
'She Repents Her Folly' blamed the man who 'induced Miss Flack to wed him' and reported he fled lynching.
One-line weekly brief: 'the bigamist has probably been lynched'.
Headline 'Wasn't Even an Honest Negro' and a brief calling Flack his 'victim' cast Sams as a criminal.
The Cleveland Gazette (a Black weekly in the white-press index) printed the marriage as a 'social sensation' without comment.

info: Marriage and elopement about mid-September 1888 (reported Sept. 18); Flack recovered in Kentucky in late September and returned to St. Louis about Oct. 1; the date of any lynching is not given
Marriage near Jacksonville, Morgan County, Illinois; Flack found near Clinton, Ky. (A4, A6) or at Moscow, Ky. (A3, A5, A13); alleged lynching location not stated beyond the Clinton area
